d: For people reading, building or scripting Uplink: how it is built, and both of its APIs.
x: These pages are for people reading or changing Uplink's source, running their own relay, or driving the app from a script. Everything here is open source under the AGPL-3.0: github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging . For how to use the app, see the docs . The source How the app is built The major parts, where each lives, and what it talks to. How the parts work together A text, a message, a call, pairing and a plugin, followed from the tap to the wire. Build, test and run it The app and the relay from source, the tests, the scripts, and how the code is commented. APIs API overview and Postman The two APIs, how each is reached and signed, and one collection of both. App API Control a running app: every method, what it takes and what it answers. Relay server API The relay's HTTP routes: files, the Marketplace, feedback and the rest. The hub and pairing protocols What an app says to the relay over a WebSocket. Making a plugin? Plugins need none of this: a plugin is one file, written by hand. Build a plugin is where that starts.

d: The major parts of Uplink, where each lives in the source, and what it talks to.
x: Uplink is one Flutter app for Android, iPhone, Mac, Windows, Linux and the browser, a small relay server, and a few helper programs. This page is a map of the source for someone about to read or change it: what each part is for, where it lives, and what it talks to. Paths are from the repository's root ( github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging ). Screens lib/ui, lib/kit, packages/glacier; lib/web starts them in a browser Texts lib/sms.dart People lib/friends, lib/me, lib/account Circles, spaces, calls lib/circles, lib/voice, lib/files Other networks lib/inbox Plugins lib/plugins, lib/market Whoever answers the screens Android itself, a paired phone, or the app alone (a browser included) Routes lib/net: the switchboard, forward secrecy, the hub route, the direct route, the SMS route Native code android/, ios/, macos/, windows/, linux/, native/voicefx, native/p2p Relay server relay/: hub, other relays, pairing, files, Marketplace, the app in a browser Helper programs sidecar/, discord/, extension/ Where things are Folder What it holds lib/ The app, in Dart, for every platform. lib/web is its start in a browser. web/ The page the browser build is loaded by: index.html with its policy, the loader, and argon2id.js , the one piece of JavaScript it carries. android/ The Android half, in Kotlin: SMS and MMS, notifications, encryption keys, the link to paired computers, the Google Messages bridge, bubbles, a friend's call ringing, the updater. ios/ , macos/ , windows/ , linux/ Each platform's runner, with the native pieces the app calls: call recording, captions, transcripts, voice messages, sounds, updates, deep links. Windows' are C++ files in windows/runner ( call_recorder.cpp , speech.cpp , desk_sound.cpp , ducking.cpp ). native/voicefx The microphone's noise removal, gain and live voice effects, in C (RNNoise, DeepFilterNet where built in, and Signalsmith Stretch behind stretch.cpp ), shared by every platform. native/p2p The direct route's core, in Rust on iroh: a node that opens framed streams to another node by its id. It carries bytes and decides nothing; every rule is Dart . native/link-check A Rust program that starts or dials a link helper and links two nodes through it, to prove one works. packages/glacier Glacier, the UI kit the screens are drawn with. A copy; it is changed in its own repository. relay/ The relay server: a Dart program with no dependencies beyond Dart's own library. relay/deploy holds what running one needs: a compose file for relay/Dockerfile , sample web server blocks, service files and relay.env.example . sidecar/ Go programs the app runs beside itself, one for each network that needs one: Google Messages, Signal, WhatsApp, Matrix, Messenger, Instagram, Discord, X and Slack. ( sidecar/linkedin is in the tree; the app doesn't offer LinkedIn.) discord/ A Node program: the bot that shows a Discord server's voice channels and bridges one into a space. Not the helper for Discord's own chats, which is sidecar/discord . extension/ The browser extension , in TypeScript: it reads the sign-in cookies of the networks signed in to in the browser and keeps them, sealed, for the account's devices. tool/ Build, release and deploy scripts, asset generators, the browser build's own checks ( tool/web ), and tests that run against a live relay ( tool/net ). site/ , docs-src/ gogho.st and these docs. docs-src is the source; tool/build-docs.mjs writes site/docs . docs/ Maintainers' notes, one per large feature: the network ( network.md ), direct links, relays that talk and the browser ( OPEN_NETWORK.md ), forward secrecy ( FORWARD_SECRECY.md ), running a relay ( SELF_HOSTING.md ), the desktop link, friends, groups, the Marketplace. examples/plugins Example plugins in the ghost-plugin/1 format. test/ , integration_test/ The app's tests, and the pictures its screen tests are held to ( test/shots ). One app, several ways of running Every screen asks for what it needs through one object, Sms.instance ( lib/sms.dart ): the conversations, a thread's messages, sending, the settings. Sms passes each call by name to whatever is set as Sms.calls , and which object that is decides how the app runs . The screens are the same in every case. Answered by Where Used when The platform channel ghost_messaging/sms lib/sms.dart , android/…/MainActivity.kt An Android phone. Kotlin reads and writes Android's own SMS and MMS database. OverlayCalls lib/standalone/overlay.dart Android, wrapped round the channel: conversations with @username friends are answered in Dart, the rest passed on. StandaloneCalls lib/standalone/standalone.dart An iPhone, a computer with no phone linked, or a browser: the app's own network and nothing from a phone. What it keeps is behind StandaloneStore ( lib/standalone/store.dart ): a folder and the Keychain ( StandaloneFiles ), or in a browser sealed records in IndexedDB ( WebStandaloneStore , lib/web/store.dart ). LinkCalls lib/desktop/remote.dart A computer paired with an Android phone: each call becomes a sealed request to the phone. DeskOwnCalls lib/desktop/own_calls.dart A paired computer the phone has handed its identity to: friends and circles run on the computer itself, texts still come from the phone. lib/main.dart chooses: a computer goes to desktopMain() ( lib/desktop/main.dart ), an iPhone starts on its own, and Android starts on the channel. A browser's build has its own entry, lib/web/main.dart , which goes to lib/web/app.dart . From there both paths load the person's choices ( AppState , lib/app_state.dart ), the plugins, the API, and then the network through startPeople ( lib/people.dart ), which starts the routes, friends, what checks the relay, groups, spaces and circles in that order. Texts on Android The app keeps no copy of your texts: they live in Android's SMS and MMS database, which is why changing texting apps loses nothing. The Kotlin side is in android/app/src/main/kotlin/com/infamousvague/ghostmessaging . File What it does MainActivity.kt Answers the channel's calls and sends events back ( ghost_messaging/events ): a conversation changed, something to open. Store.kt Reads and writes Android's database: the list, threads, messages, contacts. Messaging.kt Sending ( Sender ) and the receivers for texts arriving, MMS arriving, and sent and delivered reports. Pdu.kt The MMS wire format, written and read by hand. Notifier.kt , NotifyHush.kt , MarkdownPlain.kt Notifications, with Reply and Mark as read. None is shown for a text the list hides: the plugins' rules are written down for Kotlin by lib/plugins/notify_hush.dart , since the app may be closed when a text arrives. A preview's formatting markers are taken out. Bubbles.kt , BubbleActivity.kt A conversation as a bubble at the side of the screen, in a Flutter engine of its own started at bubbleMain ( lib/main.dart , lib/bubble.dart ). IncomingCall.kt A friend's call as a phone shows one: Answer and Decline, full screen while the phone is locked. E2e.kt , E2eCrypto.kt Encrypted texts with one person, and the phone's key pair, held under the Android Keystore. GmBridge.kt , GmWeb.kt Running beside Google Messages : reading its notifications, or its web connection through sidecar/gmessages . Desk.kt , DeskSession.kt , DeskCrypto.kt , DeskService.kt The phone's half of the link to paired computers . Routes: how apps reach each other Everything between two Uplink apps (a friend's message, a call's setup, a space's chat) goes through lib/net . Its idea is the route : one way of getting bytes to another install, behind an interface ( Carrier , lib/net/carrier.dart ) so a new one can be added without the app above knowing. Part Where What it does Envelope and packet lib/net/packet.dart An envelope is a small JSON message with a kind ( text , call , room , hello …). A packet is an envelope as a route carries it: a byte of version and flags, the sender's 16-byte name, then the envelope, sealed. The flags say whether it is sealed, a part, sealed for forward secrecy, or passed on unopened by another device of the account. Long ones cross a short route in parts. The switchboard lib/net/switchboard.dart Chooses a route for each thing sent, falls back to the next, seals and opens, joins parts, drops second copies, and answers what asks for an answer. The hub route lib/net/hub_carrier.dart , hub_link.dart A connection to the relay server's hub. Also where presence and rooms come from. Its protocol . What carries the connection is behind HubLink : dart:io 's WebSocket on a phone or a computer ( hub_link_io.dart ), the browser's own in a page ( hub_link_web.dart ). The direct route lib/net/p2p , native/p2p Packets straight between devices, with no server between. Below . The SMS route lib/net/sms_carrier.dart , android/…/NetSms.kt Packets as data texts: 133 bytes each, six at most, costing a text each, and able to wake a closed app. Keys and sealing lib/net/crypto.dart , fast_gcm.dart , android/…/Net.kt P-256 key agreement, HKDF-SHA256 and AES-256-GCM. Kotlin and Dart are held to the same bytes by tests on both sides. fast_gcm.dart has two halves that give the same bytes: one for 64-bit integers, one for a browser's. Forward secrecy lib/net/forward_secrecy.dart Prekeys each device makes and deletes, and the sealing under a one-off key for each packet. Below . Where people live lib/net/home_record.dart , homes.dart , relay_ask.dart , relay_choice.dart The signed record of which relay an account uses, looking a username up on another relay, and moving to a relay of one's own. Below . Checking the relay lib/net/ledger.dart , name_watch.dart What the relay says, compared with what friends' devices say. Below . The app's hold on it all lib/net/net.dart Net : starts the routes, knows who can be reached, and is what the rest of the app sends through. The routes are tried in the person's order ( Settings › Routes , drawn by lib/ui/network.dart ); where they have chosen none it is the hub, the direct route, the local network, then SMS ( Switchboard.order ). One is passed over when it is off, down, can't reach that person, can't hold the packet, or costs money and the message isn't one allowed to. Three routes are written: the hub, the direct route and SMS. The order names a local-network route ( lan ) that has no carrier yet. Forward secrecy A packet to a friend used to be sealed with the pair's key alone, which comes from the two accounts' long-term keys. Whoever later learned an account's words and had kept the packets could open them all. ForwardSecrecy ( lib/net/forward_secrecy.dart ) closes that: Each device makes a key pair of its own, a prekey , that is never in the account's backup. It makes a new one every day and deletes each one's private half after fifteen days. A device offers its newest prekey inside the sealed envelopes it sends ( Envelope.fs ), so no server is needed and a relay that knows nothing of it carries it. A packet to someone whose devices have offered prekeys is sealed under a key pair made for that packet alone and forgotten after. The pair's key still goes into the sealing, which is what says who sent it. To a build from before, or over a route that carries only small packets (a data text), the switchboard seals the old way. A device that can't open a forward-secret packet answers with its prekey (envelope kind fsk ) so the next try reaches it. A circle's key is changed when someone is put out of it ( lib/circles/circle_keys.dart ). docs/FORWARD_SECRECY.md in the repository is the whole design. The direct route The direct route ( P2pCarrier , id p2p , shown as Direct) carries the same sealed packets between devices themselves. The relay still comes first: it is the fast path and the one that keeps things for someone who is away. Direct is a way through when the relay can't carry something, and what the relay is checked over. Part Where What it does The core native/p2p (Rust, on iroh) A node: a key made on the device, whose public half is its node id. It dials, gets through NATs, falls back

d: Things followed from the tap to the wire: a text, a message to a friend, a call, an open space's floor, pairing a computer, adding a plugin, and more.
x: The quickest way into the source is to follow one thing through it. Here are several, each from the tap to the wire, naming the file at every step. How the app is built says what each part is. Sending a text On an Android phone where Uplink is the texting app. The box decides lib/ui/thread.dart : words alone to one friend go by the routes (the next section). Anything else is a text: Sms.instance.send . Dart to Kotlin lib/sms.dart passes send to Sms.calls . On Android that is the overlay ( lib/standalone/overlay.dart ), which passes a phone number on to the channel ghost_messaging/sms , answered in MainActivity.kt . Sender chooses SMS or MMS Sender.send in Messaging.kt . One person and no attachment is an SMS, sealed first by E2e.kt where encryption is on with them. Several people, or a picture, is an MMS, which Pdu.kt encodes. Android's database, then the radio Store.kt writes the message to Android's own database, and Android's SmsManager sends it. Reports of sent and delivered come back to SmsStatusReceiver . The screen hears Bus.changed sends an event up ghost_messaging/events ; Sms.instance.changes fires and the thread and list read again. A text arriving runs the other way: SmsDeliverReceiver in Messaging.kt writes it, Notifier.kt shows it (unless the list hides that kind of text: NotifyHush.kt ), paired computers are told, and the screen hears the same event. A message to a friend Kept first Friends.sendText ( lib/friends/friends.dart ) stores the message where the person's texts are, so it is in the conversation whether or not it has gone. Into an envelope An Envelope of kind text goes to Net.send ( lib/net/net.dart ), and on to Switchboard.send . Sealed The switchboard ( lib/net/switchboard.dart ) adds this device's prekey to the envelope. Where the friend's devices have offered prekeys of their own it seals the envelope for forward secrecy: ForwardSecrecy.sealAway ( lib/net/forward_secrecy.dart ) makes a key pair for this packet alone and wraps the envelope's key for each of their devices. Otherwise it seals with the key the two installs share. Either way the result is wrapped as a packet ( lib/net/packet.dart ). Routed The routes are tried in order. A message isn't allowed to cost money, so the SMS route is passed over and the hub comes first. The next section says how the choice is made. Through the hub HubCarrier.send ( lib/net/hub_carrier.dart ) hands it to the relay's hub ( relay/lib/hub.dart ), which passes it to the friend's connected devices, or keeps it and says so. Where nobody of that name is on this relay and the friend's home record names another, the hub gives it to Federation.pass ( relay/lib/federation.dart ), and that relay hands it on or keeps it as its own. Answered, or waited for Passed on, the sender waits a few seconds for the other app's answer and marks the message delivered. Kept, it is marked sent, and the friend's closed app is woken: an Android phone by an empty data text (at most one every ten minutes), an iPhone by a push from relay/lib/pushes.dart . Friends sends again what stays unanswered. On the other side The packet arrives at Switchboard , which joins its parts, opens it (a forward-secret one with the prekey it names), drops it if it has been seen before, and answers. A device that can't open it, because it was sealed for another device of the account, passes it on unopened to the account's own name. Friends stores it, and the conversation changes. The hub or a direct link How Switchboard.send chooses between the relay and the direct route , where a build has the direct route's core. The candidates Switchboard.routes takes the routes in the person's order (the hub, then Direct, then SMS, where they chose none) and leaves out any that is switched off, not up, doesn't reach this person, can't hold the packet, or costs money for something not worth it. P2pCarrier.reaches is true only where Direct is on and an unexpired device card is held for one of their devices. The hub first The hub takes the packet and says one of two things: passed on, or kept. Passed on, the answer from the other app is waited for, and that is the end of it. Kept: only by a link already open Kept means they are away from the relay. The direct route is then given the packet only where a stream to one of their devices is open right now ( LiveLinks.linked ), by that stream and without waiting. Nothing is dialled and no node is started for someone who is away. The same holds where the hub passed the packet on and no answer came in time. The hub can't take it: dial Where the hub is down or refuses the packet, the switchboard goes on to Direct. P2pCarrier.send ( lib/net/p2p/p2p_carrier.dart ) starts the node if it is a phone's, and sends to every device a card is held for: on an open stream, else dialled by where that device last said it was, five seconds for all of it. Where another route can still carry an envelope, P2p.meet also asks the device to bring its node up and say where it is now. Passed if one device took it; otherwise it throws and the switchboard tries the next route. Whose stream it is A stream opens with each end's nonce, then each end's proof: an HMAC under a key only the two accounts' devices hold, over both accounts, both node ids and both nonces. Until the proof has come nothing is sent or taken. What arrives after is taken as from the account whose card names that node, as the hub's stamp is. Written down The switchboard tells the ledger ( lib/net/ledger.dart ) which route took the packet and what the route said. The next time a direct stream to that friend opens, the two ledgers compare, and anything the relay said it passed that never came is sent again straight. Where this runs Tests run all of it against a stand-in node ( test/support/fake_p2p.dart ). In an app, steps three to six happen only once a build gives Net.p2pNode a node; until then the hub is followed by SMS alone. Adding a friend on another relay The name is split Buddies.add ( lib/friends/buddies.dart ) takes maya@relay.example apart. A name with no relay, or with this app's own, is asked of its own relay's directory as ever. Asked through its own relay Homes.whois ( lib/net/homes.dart ) asks the app's relay, which asks the other over a link between the two ( relay/lib/federation.dart ). The answer is their name, key and home record. Or asked directly Where the app's relay links with nobody, or couldn't reach that one, whoisAt ( lib/net/relay_ask.dart ) dials the other relay's hub itself, signed in under a key made for this one question and thrown away. Nothing of the account goes there. The record is checked HomeRecord.check ( lib/net/home_record.dart ) holds the record to the key it came with: the name is the key's, the signature is the key's. With no record, or a relay that passes nothing on, the app says they can't be reached and sends nothing. The request goes The friend request is an ordinary sealed envelope to their name. The app's hub finds nobody of that name connected, sees their record names another relay, and passes the packet there. The other relay takes it because the sender's own record names the relay it came from. Records kept in step The two friends send each other their own home records in sealed home envelopes, and again whenever one moves. A friend's app follows the record with the highest count. Joining a call in a space Allowed? Voice.join ( lib/voice/channels.dart ) checks the hub is reachable and the circle's roles allow voice, and leaves any call already on. The microphone RtcMedia ( lib/voice/rtc.dart ) opens it, with noise removal from native/voicefx in the capture path. On Android a foreground service ( CallService.kt ) keeps the call alive with the screen off. Into the room VoiceSession.join ( lib/voice/voice.dart ) joins the space's room on the hub with the name and token made from the space's seed. The hub answers with who is there, and, where the relay has a TURN server, a username and password for it that stop working after a while ( relay/lib/turn.dart ; kept as HubCarrier.callRelay ). An offer to each The newcomer makes a WebRTC connection to each member and says an offer in the room, sealed with the space's key. Each answers, and both sides exchange candidates the same way. A path is found Each connection is given the public STUN servers and the TURN server ( RtcMedia.iceServers ). Where a TURN server was handed out the connection starts through it alone, which connects whatever routers are between the two; if that fails, the side that offered starts over trying every path at once ( FallbackMedia , VoiceSession._failed ). With none handed out, it is direct paths only. Sound, between the members From there the call's sound and picture go between the members' devices, or through the TURN server, which passes packets it can't open. The hub carried the setup and carries none of the call. Kept connected VoiceSession looks at every member every two seconds. Where a connection is missing, failed, or has been finding its way too long, one of the two offers a new one: the lower id first, the other if it never does, further apart each time. Two offers that cross are settled by id. When a device's own connection to the hub drops and comes back, the carrier joins the room again and the session offers to everyone anew, since they were told it went. Nobody has to leave and come back. Ringing one friend is the same call with no space made: FriendCalls.call ( lib/voice/friend_calls.dart ) makes the call's seed from the two friends' names, joins it, and sends a sealed voice envelope by the routes. Every device of the friend's rings (on Android through IncomingCall.kt ); the one that answers tells the account's other devices to stop. An open space's floor An open space is an ordinary call ( VoiceSession , joined as above) with a floor on top. The floor is the app's alone: the relay passes its messages as it passes the call's offers, sealed, and knows nothing of places or groups. The model is lib/voice/open_space.dart ( OpenWorld , OpenSpace , OpenSpaces ), the drawing lib/ui/open_space_view.dart , the chat's bubbles lib/ui/open_space_chat.dart . The kind A space's kind travels as k wherever the space goes (its JSON, its link, the circle's manifest); an open space's is open ( SpaceKind.open , lib/voice/voice.dart ). SpaceKind.of reads a kind it doesn't know as voice , so a build from before open spaces sees one on its own as a plain call where everyone is heard whole, and in a circle as a chat. The floor appears Voice.join ( lib/voice/channels.dart ) calls OpenSpaces.follow before the relay has answered, so the floor (an OpenSpace over the session) is there from the first frame. Every surface that draws a call asks OpenSpaces.isCall(session) , which looks only at the space's kind, and draws OpenSpaceFloor in place of the call's people: the phone's page and the computer's pane in lib/ui/hangout_screen.dart , the stage beside the list, and inlineSpaceCall in lib/ui/space_designs , which draws no call page for it. Should a frame come before the floor is made, OpenSpaceFloor says the call is coming in rather than draw anything like another kind of call. Where each person stands A place is an os message, {t: 'os', x, y, d, w} : where on the 2400 by 1600 floor, which way they face in degrees, and w: 1 while walking. VoiceSession.sayPlace seals it with the space's key and says it in the call's room on the hub, as the call's offers go. It is said on coming in, whenever someone new joins the call, at most every 100 ms while walking, once on stopping, and every 3 seconds while standing still ( OpenSpace.beatEvery ), for whoever missed it. VoiceSession hands os and osg to onPlace ; an older build's switch has no case for them and drops them. Someone who never says a place (an older build, a browser guest, the Discord bridge) stands at OpenWorld.middle . Each device draws the others eased towards where they last said. Distance into loudness Whenever anyone moves, OpenS

d: Running the app and the relay from source, the tests, the scripts, and how the code is commented.
x: Everything is in one repository, github.com/InfamousVague/ghost-messaging , under the AGPL-3.0. A build from source isn't signed as the releases are, so it installs as a separate app beside the real one. What you need Flutter (stable), which brings Dart. The relay uses the same Dart and nothing else. For Android: the Android SDK and a phone or emulator. For a Mac or iPhone build: Xcode. Node for the scripts in tool/ , the Discord bot and the browser extension; Go only to build the helper programs in sidecar/ . Rust only for the direct route's core and the link helper. native/p2p/rust-toolchain.toml pins the version (1.94.1), and tool/build-p2p.sh stops with any other. For the browser build's end-to-end test: Playwright's Chromium and WebKit ( npx playwright install chromium webkit ). Run it flutter pub get flutter run # on the connected phone, or -d macos / windows / linux flutter build apk --release --target-platform android-arm64 flutter build macos A computer's build starts in lib/desktop/main.dart ; with no phone paired it runs on its own, with an account and no texts. The app talks to the relay at gogho.st unless Settings › Routes is given another. The helper programs for other networks are not built by flutter run . Build the one you want first ( tool/build-signalsidecar.sh , tool/build-accountsidecar.sh messenger mac …): on a computer the app looks for it beside itself and then under build/ name -sidecar/ , where those scripts put it. Build it for a browser node tool/build-web.mjs # into build/web, to be served under /app/ by a relay dart run relay/bin/relay.dart --web build/web # then open http://127.0.0.1:8787/app/ node tool/web/e2e.mjs # two people using it, in Chromium and then WebKit tool/build-web.mjs is flutter build web -t lib/web/main.dart with what the page needs said for it: the engine served from the build's own folder, no code made from text at run time, no service worker, and main.dart.js named by its hash. Before it builds it runs test/web_build_test.dart (the page's policy, its files and its headers) and tool/web/check-argon2.mjs (the Argon2id worker against test/vectors/argon2id.json ). Its options: Option What it does --base /app/ Where the page will be served from. --hub wss://…/hub The hub it speaks to. With none it speaks to the hub beside the page: /hub where the page is /app/ . --out folder Somewhere other than build/web . --profile Names kept in the JavaScript, for reading what went wrong. Letters the app's own fonts have no shape for (Chinese, Arabic, mathematics…) are drawn from Noto fonts served beside the page, never fetched from Google by a visitor's browser. node tool/web/fallback-fonts.mjs --fetch brings them to build/fallback-fonts once; without them such letters are boxes. web/argon2id.js is committed, and tool/web/build-argon2.mjs builds it again from the extension's pinned packages. Run the relay cd relay dart pub get # the test package only dart run bin/relay.dart --port 8787 --verbose # ws://127.0.0.1:8787/hub and /relay/ channel dart compile exe bin/relay.dart -o ghost-relay # one file to run on a server It listens on this machine alone unless given --host , keeps everything under --data ( relay-data ), and serves the browser build under /app/ with --web folder . Every other choice is a variable in its environment, and none is required: relay/deploy/relay.env.example lists them all, grouped by what each switches on. Put it behind a web server that holds the certificate and passes everything to it, WebSockets included: /hub , /relay/* , /files* , /market* , /link/* , /word/* , /feedback , and /app/* where it serves the app. relay/deploy has samples for Caddy and nginx, a systemd service, and a compose file that runs relay/Dockerfile with Caddy in front. Then point an app at it: Settings › Routes takes the hub's address. To switch on Set Passing packets to other relays GHOST_FED=open or list , with GHOST_PUBLIC_HUB , the address other relays dial to check yours. Off by default. Sign-ins bound to your relay's host GHOST_HUB_NAMES Calls through a TURN server GHOST_TURN_SECRET and GHOST_TURN_URLS , for a coturn you run with the same secret ( relay/deploy/turnserver.conf.example ). Link helpers for direct links GHOST_LINK_HELPERS , for an iroh-relay you run (below). The app in a browser --web or GHOST_WEB_DIR docs/SELF_HOSTING.md in the repository is the full guide, and says what a relay of your own does and doesn't reach. Running your own has the short version. The direct route's core and a link helper sh tool/build-p2p.sh mac # build/p2p/mac/libghost_p2p.dylib; also: android, ios (cd native/p2p cargo test --release --locked) sh tool/build-link.sh host # build/link/host/iroh-relay, for this machine (cd native/link-check cargo run) # starts that helper and links two nodes through it native/p2p builds to one library with a small C interface ( include/ghost_p2p.h ), which lib/net/p2p/node_ffi.dart loads. d: The two APIs, how each is reached and signed, and a Postman collection of both.
x: Uplink has two APIs. The app's API controls one running app: its conversations, plugins, other networks and screens. The relay server's API is what every app speaks to the server that carries messages between them. Both are documented in full here, and both are in one Postman collection. The Postman collection ghost-messaging.postman_collection.json (Postman's v2.1 format; Insomnia, Bruno and others read it too). In Postman: Import , then choose the file or paste its address, https://gogho.st/docs/api/ghost-messaging.postman_collection.json . It holds every method of the app's API and every HTTP route of the relay, each with its parameters described and an example body. It is made from the same lists these pages are drawn from, so it matches them. Set its variables before the first call: Variable Starts as What it is app http://127.0.0.1:8765 Where the app serves its API ( Turn it on ). token empty The app's token, from Settings › API › Copy the token . Sent as Authorization: Bearer on every app request. relay https://gogho.st The relay server. Your own, if you run one. filesToken empty A Files space's token, for the Files routes. ghostKey , ghostTime , ghostSig empty The signing headers of a signed relay route (below). Signed routes Some relay routes are signed with an install's private key, over the request's method, path, time and body. Postman can't make that signature by itself, so those requests carry the headers as variables for you to fill from your own code. Signing a request says exactly what is signed. Routes anyone may read work as they are. The hub and the pairing channels are WebSockets with binary frames, which a collection of HTTP requests can't hold. They are written out in The hub and pairing protocols . The app's API Where On the device, http://127.0.0.1:8765 (the port can be changed); on your network too where allowed; from anywhere through the relay, sealed. Who may call Whoever holds the token (HTTP) or the connection string (through the relay). Off until turned on in developer mode. Shape POST /api/ method with the parameters as a JSON object. Answers {"ok": true, "result": …} or {"ok": false, "error": {"code", "message"}} . Reference App API : every method. The relay server's API Where https://gogho.st , or any server running relay/ . Who may call Anyone, for what is public (the Marketplace's catalog). A Files space's routes need its token. Routes that change something are signed with an install's key. Shape Plain HTTP with JSON or raw bytes, for files, the Marketplace and feedback. WebSockets for the hub and pairing. Reference Relay server API (HTTP) and The hub and pairing protocols (WebSocket). What the relay can and can't see The relay is built to carry what it can't read. Packets, rooms' chat, calls' setup, files and account backups are sealed on the device with keys the server never holds. It sees which installs connect, which talk to which, when, and how much. It knows an install by a name made from its public key, and keeps usernames, linked handles and numbers as hashes. Privacy and safety says the same for people who aren't reading the source.
h: What the relay can and can't see

d: Control the app from a script or another program: every method, what it takes and what it answers.
x: Uplink has an API: every part of the app, from your conversations to its screens, as methods you can call from a script or another program. It's off until you turn it on, and only someone with your token or connection string can use it. Turn it on Developer mode On your phone, tap Settings › About › Version twelve times. Taps more than two seconds apart start the count again, and from the eighth tap a note counts down. Then Settings › Developer and Settings › API appear. Choose how to reach it API On this phone Serve the API Over HTTP, with a token Allow from Wi-Fi Served on the phone's address on your network too Copy the token From anywhere Through the relay Copy the connection string Serve the API : over HTTP on the phone. From a computer by USB: adb forward tcp:8765 tcp:8765 , then call http://localhost:8765 . Allow from Wi-Fi serves it on your network too. Through the relay : from anywhere. The connection string ( ghostapi1:… ) holds the key every call is sealed with; the relay passes calls along without being able to read them. Keep it as you would a password. Call a method Over HTTP, POST /api/ method with the parameters as a JSON body and your token: curl -s http://localhost:8765/api/conversations.list \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer token ' \ -d '{"limit": 5}' Or with the command-line client in the app's repository ( tool/ghost-api.mjs ): node tool/ghost-api.mjs --token token app.info node tool/ghost-api.mjs --remote ghostapi1: secret networks.chats '{"network": "telegram"}' With no method it lists them all; --doc method shows one's documentation. Requests and answers Request What it does GET /api Everything the API says of itself: every method, as JSON ( api.describe ). GET /api/ method One method's documentation. POST /api/ method Calls it. The body is its parameters as a JSON object, or empty. POST /api The same as one object: {"method": "…", "params": {…}, "id": …} . The id comes back with the answer. Every request but GET / needs Authorization: Bearer token . Answers are JSON: {"ok": true, "result": …} {"ok": false, "error": {"code": "bad_params", "message": "\"thread\" is needed: …"}} Code Status Meaning unauthorized 401 The token is missing or wrong. not_found 404 No such method, or what it named isn't there. bad_params 400 A parameter is missing or of the wrong type, or the body isn't a JSON object. Also 405 for anything but GET and POST. failed 500 The method ran and what it asked failed. The message says why. Parameter types are string , int , bool , list and object , and each call is checked against them before it runs. Through the relay The connection string is ghostapi1: and 64 hex digits: a secret of 32 bytes. Both ends make three things from it with HKDF-SHA256 (salt ghost-api v1 ): the pairing channel they meet on (info relay channel , its first 16 bytes), that channel's token ( relay token ), and an AES-256-GCM key ( seal key ). The app holds the channel as its phone end; a client joins as the other ( Pairing channels ). A request is one binary frame: a 12-byte nonce, then {"method", "params", "id"} sealed with the key (additional data ghost-api-v1 , GCM's tag at the end). The answer comes back the same way. The relay passes the frames and can't open them. The app must be running to answer. tool/ghost-api.mjs is a client of about 150 lines to read or copy from. The methods Settings › API › Methods lists the same, with a place to try each. Those marked changes things send, delete or change something, and ask before running there. d: The relay server's HTTP routes: files, the Marketplace, feedback and the rest.
x:
The relay is mostly two WebSockets, the hub and the pairing relay. Beside them it answers a small set of plain HTTP routes: a circle's sealed files, the plugin Marketplace, feedback, bounties, the pages that link a handle, and, where it is given the folder, the app built for a browser. This page lists every one. Relays that talk to each other, home records and a call's media relay have no HTTP routes of their own: they are spoken over the hub's socket. The public relay is at https://gogho.st . Anyone can run their own from the source: dart run relay/bin/relay.dart --port 8787 . The WebSocket protocols are on The hub and pairing protocols , and a Postman collection of these routes is on API overview and Postman . Conventions CORS for one address, on two routes. These routes are for the app and for scripts, not for a page in a browser on another site: the relay sets no Access-Control-* header, but for the two things the app in a browser sends from an address of its own, POST /feedback and POST /market/abuse . A relay set with that address ( GHOST_APP_ORIGIN ) answers both with Vary: Origin , and, to a request whose Origin is exactly that address, with Access-Control-Allow-Origin naming it. An OPTIONS from that origin is answered 204 with Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST , Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, x-ghost-key, x-ghost-time, x-ghost-sig, x-ghost-body-sha256, x-ghost-body-length and Access-Control-Max-Age: 600 . No other route, and no other origin, is told anything. No match is not an error. A request that fits no route, whatever its method, answers 200 with the plain text Ghost Messaging relay . There is no separate health route: this is it. JSON answers are application/json; charset=utf-8 . Request bodies are read as UTF-8 JSON or raw bytes; no Content-Type is looked at. Hex is lowercase. Ids and hashes in paths must match their shape exactly, or the route does not exist. Times are whole milliseconds since 1970, as decimal digits. Per-address limits on these routes go by the first value of X-Forwarded-For , or the connection's address where there is none. The hub counts differently: see Signing in to the hub . Each module says no in its own shape: Module A refusal Notes Files {"err": "No such space."} A sentence. A few carry more: have , done , seq . Feedback {"error": "Feedback is sent with POST."} A sentence, under error , not err . Marketplace {"ok": false, "error": "not_found", "message": "There's nothing here by that name."} error is a fixed code; message is for people. Every success carries "ok": true . Bounties {"error": "Not here."} A sentence, under error , as feedback's. The app in a browser Not found Plain text with 404 . A wrong method is 405 with no body. Outside the modules, a path or a query whose percent-escapes are not UTF-8 answers 400 with no body, and an error nothing else caught answers 500 with no body. Both close the connection. Signing a request Writes to Files, feedback, and most of the Marketplace are signed with the install's own key, the same one the hub knows it by. No account or password is involved. A bounty is signed the same way, by one key the relay was given. Thing Format Key P-256 (secp256r1). The public key is 33 bytes compressed: 02 or 03 , then x. In a header it is standard base64 with padding, 44 characters. Signature ECDSA over the SHA-256 of the signed string. 64 bytes: r (32, big-endian) then s (32). Not DER. Standard base64, 88 characters. Id The first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of the 33 key bytes, as 32 lowercase hex digits. This is who the relay says wrote something. Body hash SHA-256 of the body's bytes, 64 lowercase hex digits. For an empty body: e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855 . All three modules take the same three headers and sign five lines joined by a line feed ( 
 ), as UTF-8, with no line feed after the last. Only the first line and a few rules differ. x-ghost-key: base64 of the 33-byte public key x-ghost-time: milliseconds since 1970 x-ghost-sig: base64 of the 64-byte signature The relay remembers what each key signed, so the same request sent twice is refused the second time. To try again, sign again with a new time. Files Every Files route but GET /files also carries the space's token: Authorization: Ghost token , 64 lowercase hex digits. Reads need only the token. Writes need the token and the signature. ghost-files v1 METHOD path and query, as sent time body sha256 hex The third line is the whole request target, query included: /files/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/log?after=7 . The time may be up to 10 minutes from the relay's clock, either way. Where the body is not read ( DELETE /files/{space} , POST …/done ), sign the empty body's hash. For a blob's piece sent with x-ghost-body-sha256 , the last line is that header's value, and the signature is checked before the body is read. Any failure answers 401 {"err": "Bad signature."} . Feedback ghost-feedback v1 POST /feedback time body sha256 hex The third line is the path alone, with no query. The time may be up to 5 minutes from the relay's clock. Marketplace ghost-market v1 METHOD path time body sha256 hex The third line is the path alone. A signed request with any query string is refused. The time may be up to 5 minutes from the relay's clock. A POST must say its body up front, in two more headers: x-ghost-body-sha256 (64 lowercase hex digits; the last signed line) and x-ghost-body-length (the length in bytes, equal to Content-Length ). A chunked body is refused. A GET or DELETE must send neither of those headers and no body, and signs the empty body's hash. A missing header answers 401 unsigned . A bad key, time or signature, or a repeat, answers 401 bad_signature . A broken shape (a query, a header sent twice, a length that does not match) answers 400 bad_request . A signed GET /market/mine looks like this: GET /market/mine HTTP/1.1 Host: gogho.st x-ghost-key: AqGyw9Tl9gcYKTpLXG1+j5ChssPU5fYHGCk6S1xtfo+Q x-ghost-time: 1795000000000 x-ghost-sig: 88 base64 characters and its signature is over these bytes: ghost-market v1 GET /market/mine 1795000000000 e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855 Bounties ghost-bounty v1 POST /bounty time body sha256 hex The same three headers. x-ghost-key must be the relay's bounty key ( GHOST_BOUNTY_KEY ), not an install's. The third line is always /bounty . The time may be up to 5 minutes from the relay's clock. A repeat is refused. Any failure answers 401 {"error": "Not signed by the bounty key, or too old."} . Signatures inside Marketplace bodies Review's decisions are signed a second time, by the reviewer's key, so that the apps can check them without trusting the relay. Each is the same kind of signature over lines joined by 
 , and travels as a JSON object with exactly the fields shown. Here key and sig are strict base64: the standard alphabet, padded, no whitespace. What Signed string Object Approval ghost-market approve v1
 plugin 
 version 
 sha256 {"v": 1, "plugin", "version", "sha256", "key", "sig", "at"} Revocation ghost-market revoke v1
 plugin 
 sha256 
 at 
 why {"v": 1, "plugin", "sha256", "at", "why", "key", "sig"} Retirement ghost-market retire v1
 key (the key's base64 text) {"v": 1, "key", "at", "sig"} General The relay has one answer for anything it does not recognise. A script can use it to see that a relay is there. GET / The answer to any request, of any method and path, that no other route takes. There is no separate health route. Who Anyone Answers 200 text/plain: Ghost Messaging relay Refusals 400 (empty) a path whose percent-escapes are not UTF-8 404 text/plain: Ghost Messaging relay a WebSocket upgrade whose last path segment is neither hub nor 32 hex digits 400 (empty) a WebSocket upgrade to the hub or a channel whose Sec-WebSocket-Key is not 1 to 64 printable ASCII characters Sign-in links These are pages for a browser, not an API to call. When someone links a Discord, Telegram or X handle, the app asks the hub for a sign-in address and opens it. The address holds a state made for that install, good for 10 minutes and for one sign-in. The relay checks the sign-in with the network, links the handle, and tells the install over the hub. A network whose keys are not set on the server is off, and its page says the link is no good. GET /link/{network} Starts a sign-in the app asked for over the hub. Sends the browser to the network's own sign-in (Discord, X) or shows Telegram's login widget. Who Anyone holding a state from the hub Field Where Needed What network path yes discord, telegram or x. Anything else gets the root answer. s query yes The state the hub made for this install: 32 hex digits, good for 10 minutes. Answers 302 Location: the network's sign-in (discord, x); 200 text/html (telegram) Refusals 400 text/html That didn't work the state is unknown, expired or for another network, or that sign-in is not set up GET /link/{network}/callback Where the network sends the browser back. Checks the sign-in, links the handle, and tells the install over the hub. The state works once. Who Anyone holding a state from the hub Field Where Needed What network path yes discord, telegram or x. state query yes The state the sign-in was started with. code query discord and x: the network's authorization code. id query telegram: the widget's id. Required for telegram. auth_date query telegram: when the widget signed, in seconds. Required for telegram; at most 86400 seconds old. hash query telegram: the widget's HMAC-SHA256 over its fields. Required for telegram. username query telegram: the account's username. Also taken: first_name, last_name, photo_url. Answers 200 text/html Linked Refusals 400 text/html That didn't work the state is unknown or used, the sign-in was cancelled, the account could not be confirmed or has no username Invite words A circle can be joined by a word. The relay keeps, under the SHA-256 of the word, a sealed link of at most 1024 characters that the app gave it over the hub. It never sees the word or what the link opens. This one route is how the site's join page looks a word up. GET /word/{h} The sealed invite link kept under a word's hash. The word itself is never sent. Who Anyone Field Where Needed What h path yes SHA-256 of the word, as the app works it out: 64 lowercase hex digits. Answers 200 { b : sealed link } Refusals 404 { b : null} no such word, a hash of the wrong shape, or a method other than GET Files A space's files live on the relay as sealed blobs, beside an ordered log of sealed operations that says what the files are. The relay can't read either: names, keys and contents are sealed by the apps. It sees the space's id, each blob's size, when things were written, and the id of the install that wrote them. A space is named by an id (32 hex digits) and guarded by a token (64 hex digits), both made by the apps from the space's secret. The relay keeps only the token's hash, and a wrong token is answered exactly as a space that isn't there. Anyone with the token can read. Writing also takes a signature, so a blob is written and finished only by whoever started it, and removed by them, the space's owner, or a moderator who shows the space's signed roster. Uploading a file is three steps: reserve a blob with its size, send its pieces in order, then finish it. An upload cut short carries on from have . A blob not finished holds its room in the space until it is finished or dropped, and the space's state lists the newest hundred of them under parts , so an app can show an upload that stopped halfway and carry it on or remove it. d: What an app says to the relay server over a WebSocket: signing in, packets, presence, rooms and the directory.
x: The relay server speaks two WebSocket protocols. The hub is where installs find each other: any address ending in /hub , so wss://gogho.st/hub . A pairing channel joins one phone to one of its computers: an address ending in 32 hex digits, wss://gogho.st/relay/ channel . Both pass sealed bytes the server can't read. A third is spoken between relay servers: one relay dials another's hub and, in place of an app's sign-in, says it is a relay ( Relays that talk to each other ). Its plain HTTP routes are in the relay's HTTP routes , and how the app uses all of this is in Routes . On all of them, a text frame is one JSON object and a binary frame is a sealed packet. The server pings each socket every 30 seconds, never compresses a message, and holds every message to a length before it reads it ( Message sizes and the memory budget ). The code is relay/lib/hub.dart , relay/lib/relay.dart , relay/lib/federation.dart and relay/lib/ws_door.dart ; the app's side of the hub is lib/net/hub_carrier.dart . Who an install is An install is a P-256 (secp256r1) key pair made on the device. The hub knows it by a name made from the public key. There is no account to make first: anyone with a key can sign in. Thing What it is Public key 33 bytes, compressed: 02 or 03 , then x. Sent as base64 in the sign-in, whois and acct-put ; as 66 lowercase hex digits for a read-only room's owner . Name (id) The first 16 bytes of SHA-256 of those 33 bytes, as 32 lowercase hex digits. In binary frames it is the 16 raw bytes. Signature ECDSA over SHA-256 of the message, as 64 raw bytes: r, then s, big-endian. Not DER. Sent as base64 in the sign-in and in bind ; as 128 lowercase hex digits in a read-only room's grants. Account address An Uplink account is a second key, secp256k1, known by an Ethereum-style address: 0x and 40 hex digits. Only the account messages use it. All hex the server reads is lowercase. Signing in to the hub Open a WebSocket to wss://gogho.st/hub . With 20,000 sockets open already, the upgrade is refused with HTTP 503 . The hub speaks first, with a number made for this connection (32 random bytes, as 64 hex digits): {"hello": " 64 hex ", "peek": true, "react": true, "v2": true, "relay": {"id": " 32 hex ", "key": " base64 ", "url": "wss://relay.example.com/hub", "fed": true}} peek says this hub knows the look-only sign-in below. react says it takes reaction packets . v2 is there only on a hub that knows the hosts it is reached at, and says it takes the sign-in bound to a host, below. relay is there only on a relay that talks to other relays : its own name and key, its hub's address where it claims one ( url ), and the relay it stays linked to where it has one ( via ). Within 10 seconds, answer with one text frame of 16,384 bytes at most: {"id": " 32 hex ", "key": " base64, 33 bytes ", "sig": " base64, 64 bytes ", "device": "desk-1", "v": 2, "host": "gogho.st"} The hub answers, then hands over what it held for you as binary frames: {"ok": true, "held": 3, "now": 1763900000000, "since": 1763800000000, "helpers": ["https://…"]} now is the hub's clock and since is when it started, both in milliseconds. What a hub holds is in memory, so a packet it said it held before since is gone. helpers is there only where the relay names link helpers: up to 4 https:// addresses of servers that help two devices link directly. Field What it holds id Your name. It must be the one made from key . key Your public key, base64. sig Your signature, base64. Without v : over the 13 bytes of ghost-hub v1 (with its space) followed by the 32 raw bytes of the hub's number: the hex decoded, not the hex text. With "v": 2 : over the 13 bytes of ghost-hub v2 , one byte holding the length of host , the bytes of host in lower case, then the 32 bytes of the hub's number. v Optional. 2 for the sign-in bound to a host. Use it when the hello said "v2": true . host With "v": 2 : the host you dialled, with its port only where that is not 443 or 80. It must be one the hub is reached at, compared in lower case. device Optional. Which of your devices this is, 64 characters at most. Left out, too long or not a string, it counts as the empty string. peek Optional. true makes this a look only. mode Optional. busy or invisible : how you are shown from the first moment, where this is your name's first device here. See Presence . fed 1 from another relay, never from an app: the frame is then a relay's hello , with other fields. Bound to a host A v1 signature says nothing of where it was made, so a server an app was pointed at could pass the app's own relay's number to it and sign in there with the answer. A v2 signature is good only at a hub reached by the host it names. Once the hub has seen a key sign in with v2, it takes no v1 from that key while it knows its own hosts, and answers {"ok": false, "err": "This account signs in a newer way now: update Uplink on this device."} . Refused again within the hour, the answer comes 2 minutes late, with the connection open meanwhile. The hub remembers 200,000 such keys across restarts, letting go first of those that hold no username. A hub that knows no hosts takes v1 from anyone and never says v2 . One name can be signed in from 8 devices at once. A new connection with the same device takes the older one's place, and a ninth device takes the place of the one connected longest. The connection that lost its place is closed with 4409 . Where the hub counts what one place does, a place is the connection's address: an IPv4 address, or the first 48 bits of an IPv6 one. Behind a proxy on the same machine or a private network, it is the last address in X-Forwarded-For , the one the proxy saw. A look With "peek": true the hub says how much is waiting and closes the socket with 1000 ( looked ). Nothing is handed over or removed, and no other connection of yours is replaced. A closed app uses it to see whether it should wake. {"ok": true, "held": 3, "peek": true, "here": false} here says whether any device of this name is connected now. Refusals and close codes Code Reason When 4400 bad hello The first frame wasn't JSON text, the base64 didn't decode, id isn't made from key , or the signature is wrong. Sent first: {"ok": false, "err": "bad hello"} . Also a v2 sign-in whose host is not one of the hub's ( err is then This relay isn't reached as host . ), and a v1 sign-in from a key that signs in with v2. 4401 no hello No sign-in was accepted within 10 seconds. 4409 replaced A newer connection took this device's place. 1000 looked A look was answered. 1009 too big A binary frame was empty or longer than 65,568 bytes. 4403 The reason Another relay's hello was refused. See Linking . 4503 full The hub filled while this connection was being made. 1001 The server is stopping. None The socket is dropped with no close frame for a message past what the door takes , or a connection that holds too much. After signing in A text frame is known by its keys, tried in this order: ping , push , dir , watch , mode , away , join , anchor , leave , look , unlook . The first that matches decides. {"ping": 1} is answered {"pong": 1} , with whatever value was sent. No answer means ignored A frame that isn't a JSON object, a dir the server doesn't know, an unknown first byte and a binary frame too short for its kind all get no answer. A client can't tell ignored from lost. Packets to a person A binary frame's first byte is its kind. Kind 0x01 is a packet to one name. The payload is sealed by the apps; the hub doesn't read it. The hub puts the sender's name in itself, so nobody can send under another's. Direction Bytes Holds To the hub 0 0x01 1 to 4 seq : a number you choose, uint32, big-endian. It comes back in the answer. 5 to 20 The recipient's name, 16 bytes. 21 on The payload, one byte at least. From the hub 0 0x01 1 to 16 The sender's name, 16 bytes. 17 on The payload. A whole frame is 65,568 bytes at most (64 KiB and 32 bytes for headers). A longer one, or an empty one, closes the connection with 1009 . The packet goes to every connected device of the recipient except the connection that sent it. Each one is answered with a text frame: Answer Meaning {"ack": seq , "here": true} Passed to at least one connected device. {"ack": seq , "here": false} Nobody was there. It is held, and a push is asked for where the recipient registered one. {"nak": seq , "err": "full"} Nobody was there and it could not be held. {"ack": seq , "here": false, "fed": true} The recipient lives on another relay, and that relay took it. Whether they are connected there is never said across relays. {"ack": seq , "here": false, "fed": true, "waiting": true} The recipient lives on another relay that can't be reached just now. The packet waits on this relay until it can. {"nak": seq , "err": "home"} For another relay, but this relay holds no home record of yours that names it. Give your record and send again. {"nak": seq , "err": "busy"} For another relay, and you are past what one install may send across relays, or may make this relay dial. {"nak": seq , "err": "far"} Their relay is one this relay doesn't link with, or can't reach. {"nak": seq , "err": "refused"} Their relay would not take it. The answers with fed , and the last four refusals, come only from a relay that talks to other relays , and only for a recipient who is not connected here and whose home record names another relay. A packet you send to your own name is never passed on. Held for someone away The hub holds up to 200 frames and 1 MiB for one name, 96 MiB for everyone together, for 7 days. Against the 96 MiB each held frame counts as its bytes and 256 more. When the name next signs in, its mailbox is emptied and everything not too old is handed over, right after {"ok": true, "held": n} . An ack means the hub took the packet, not that the other app opened it. The frames are handed over in order, only as fast as the connection takes them. Any not written by the time the connection closes go back to the mailbox. A packet a device sent to its own name is not handed back to that device: it stays held for the name's other devices. Held in memory Held packets are kept in memory only. A restart of the server loses them. The since in the sign-in's answer says when the hub last started. Presence A connection asks about names with watch , and from then on is told when they come and go. Watches add up for the life of the connection, to 500 names. There is no message to stop watching. {"watch": [" id ", " id "]} Answered at once, about the names in that message: {"here": [" id "], "away": [" id "], "busy": [" id "], "seen": {" id ": 1763900000000}} Field Meaning here Names connected now. away Names connected with every device put away. busy Names connected that chose to be shown as busy. seen For names not connected, when each was last here, in milliseconds since 1970. The hub remembers this for 200,000 names. Message From Meaning {"away": true} or false You This device was put away, or is back in use. Not answered. {"came": " id "} Hub The name's first device connected. {"went": " id ", "at": ms } Hub Its last device disconnected. at is when it was put away, if it had been, else now. {"away": " id ", "is": bool , "at": ms } Hub Whether all of its devices are away has changed. {"mode": "online"} , "busy" or "invisible" You How your name is shown, said by any of its devices and held while one is connected. Any other word counts as online . Not answered. {"busy": " id ", "is": bool } Hub The name became busy, or stopped being. An invisible name is shown to its watchers as gone. They are sent went when it hides. While it hides it is in none of here , away and busy , no came or away is sent for it, and its last-seen time stays where it was. When it stops hiding, watchers are sent came , then away if its devices are put away. A mode said in the sign-in holds from the first moment, so a name that signs in invisible never shows as come.
